newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka gem industry strives to sparkle.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka gem industry strives to sparkle.

text.p: Some of the world's rarest and most expensive gemstones will be up for sale this week when international buyers gather in Colombo for "Facets 96," the annual Sri Lankan gem and jewellery show.
Sri Lanka's age-old gem industry, hit by falling production and competition from newcomers Tanzania, Vietnam and Madagascar, hopes to use the show to ensure its leading position in the world.
About 100 dealers will exhibit their products, while a similar number of buyers will vie for the best items and prices at Facets from September 9-12.

"Gems have brought us fame and fortune. And they have brought us visitors from far away," said Nowfel S. Jabir, president of the Sri Lanka Gem Traders Association and chairman of Colombo's Nowgem Jewellers.
"In Sri Lanka, gems are forever," Jabir told Reuters.
Sri Lanka boasts that it has 55 of the world's known varieties of gems, but this year's Facets will also show stones from other nations.
This underlines the needs for the local industry to move to jewellery and the cutting and polishing of imported rough stones, industry officials said.

Sri Lanka's gem exports dropped from 2.2 billion rupees ($40 million) in 1994 to 1.9 billion rupees last year. Once the third biggest foreign exchange earner for the island, the industry has now dropped to sixth place.

"We have been mining for so long, it is now difficult to raise quantities," said Tom Ellawala, chairman of the National Gem and Jewellery Authority. "We're not producing as freely and as liberally as we used to five or six years ago."
Ellawela is hard at work these days seeking uncut gems from Tanzania to be cut and polished in Sri Lanka for re-export, thus utilising the island's fully developed technology.
"It will give us a larger market without actually having to find more gems in Sri Lanka," one analyst said.
Sri Lankan law permits dealers to import rough stones and re-export cut and polished stones duty free.
"The value addition in cutting and polishing is as high as 40 percent. It can make money for the country while providing valuable employment," Jabir said.
The Central Bank said in its annual report that the volume of gem exports had declined due to low domestic production.
"The cost of mining increased mainly due to higher costs of deeper mining as well as inputs such as fuel and machinery," it said.
The bank said newcomer Madagascar and other low cost producing nations now challenged Sri Lanka, which has been known for its gems almost since the start of recorded history.
The Bible records that Solomon, the 10th century B.C. king of Israel, sent emissaries to the island to fetch gems for the beautiful Queen of Sheba.
The old story of Sindbad the Sailor tells of a Sri Lankan king's palace covered with 100,000 rubies. Sinbad was washed ashore on the island of Serendib, an old name of Sri Lanka, after a ship wreck.
Officials say the Sri Lankan gem industry's longevity may now be putting it at a disadvantage in mining, but has equipped it with skills.
About 30,000 people in Sri Lanka are engaged in the lapidary industry, cutting and polishing stones.
"The people of Sri Lanka are known for excellence in jewellery crafstmanship. They have been so from the times of the ancient kings," Jabir said.
Unlike gems, jewellery exports have been growing. In 1995, jewellery exports rose to 526 million rupees from 463 million a year ago.
($1=55 rupees)
